title: The Catalyst | May 4, 2026
intro:
Good Morning Thorium Valley, welcome back to the Catalyst Newsletter.

Today we've got a bank CEO who let his AI clone deliver 30 minutes of a Wall Street earnings call before telling anyone it wasn't him. The financials behind the stunt are what make it hard to laugh off.

We're also looking at a guy who can't write a single line of code but manages more than 30 AI agents every day, and how his actual job quietly turned into something nobody had a title for a year ago.

And then there's BCG telling companies to spend dramatically more on AI tokens, while a growing pile of research, including some tied to BCG itself, suggests that more usage doesn't actually mean better work. Meta and Salesforce already went all in on tracking it. The early results are not what anyone expected.

title: She Built 6 AI Agents. She's Never Worked Harder.
intro:
Good Morning Thorium Valley, welcome back to the Catalyst Newsletter.

Today we're talking about a product manager who built six AI agents to handle most of her daily work and then discovered she's somehow more exhausted than before, and why that's a trap worth understanding before you automate everything.

We're also looking at how a 900-person company got basically every employee building their own AI tools without writing a single line of code, and the simple support structure that made it actually stick.

And we've got a café owner who was about to kill menu items that turned out to be some of his best sellers, all because he asked AI one question about his sales data before pulling the trigger.
toc: She Built 6 AI Agents. She's Never Worked Harder.
Checkr Made 900 Non-Coders Build Their Own AI Tools
He Used Square's AI to Find a Hidden Best-Seller He Almost Cut

stories.title: She Built 6 AI Agents. She's Never Worked Harder.
stories.content:
Vivi Mengjie Xiao is an AI product manager in China who used to spend four hours a day just gathering industry news. Reading posts, translating articles, scrolling newsletters. She figured if AI could handle that, maybe it could handle more.

So she built six AI agents on OpenClaw, three for work and three for personal life. There was an admin assistant for scheduling, a researcher for synthesizing information, and a chief of staff that simulated her boss's communication style so she could rehearse presentations. On the personal side she set up a life coach, a content assistant, and a finance tracker.

The results were genuinely impressive. About 60 to 70% of her daily operational work is now handled by agents. She publishes podcast episodes daily, monitors finances in real time, manages content across multiple platforms, and runs a knowledge management system while keeping a full-time job.

Here's the thing nobody talks about though. Her bedtime shifted from midnight to 2AM. She's more productive by every metric and also more tired than she's ever been. The agents didn't give her time back. They gave her room to attempt more. "When your efficiency goes up, you don't work less," she told Business Insider. "You just attempt more."

That's the trap. You automate the grunt work, see all this new capacity, and immediately fill it with creative and strategic work you never had bandwidth for. Which sounds great until you're working more hours on harder problems with no built-in stopping point.

The pattern here is useful for anyone drowning in repetitive work whether that's weekly reports, client onboarding, data gathering, or internal comms. The key is what Vivi figured out the hard way. She initially tried cramming everything into a single agent and it basically became "ADHD like me," jumping between tasks without helping. One agent per job. Get it right, then expand.

The Formula

1. List every repeating task you do in a week. Open a Google Sheet or Notion page. Columns for the task, who does it, how often, and how long it takes. Spend some time filling this in honestly because this is your audit.

2. Flag anything that's pure information work. Research, summarizing, reformatting documents, distributing content, updating one spreadsheet from another. These are your first candidates.

3. Pick one task and build a Claude Project around it. Go to Claude, create a Project, upload your templates or examples, and write instructions for how you want it done. Treat it like onboarding a new hire and be specific about the output you expect.

4. Run it for a week before adding the next one. Vivi's biggest lesson was that one overloaded agent is useless. Get the first workflow reliable, then add the second. Each one should have its own Project with its own context.

5. Decide what you're doing with the freed time before you free it. Otherwise you will fill it with more work and end up more productive and more exhausted. That's not a hypothetical, that's exactly what happened here.

Have Claude Explain This to Me

Copy this prompt into Claude:

A product manager was spending hours each day on repetitive operational
work like research, content distribution, and admin tasks. She built 6
specialized AI agents to handle about 70% of that work, freeing herself
up for creative and strategic projects but also working longer hours
because she kept filling the freed time with more ambitious tasks.

Here's the basic approach from Thorium Valley:
- Audit every repeating task you do in a week with what it is, how
  often, and how long it takes
- Flag anything that's pure information gathering, formatting, or
  distribution as your first automation candidates
- Build one Claude Project per workflow with specific instructions
  and example outputs
- Get each workflow reliable before adding the next one
- Decide upfront what you'll do with freed time so you don't just
  pile on more work

Thorium Valley and heard you're trying to figure out which parts of
your work to hand off to AI. Could I get a little more context on:
1. What does a typical week look like for you, and which tasks eat
   the most time without requiring much of your judgment?
2. What would you actually want to spend more time on if the
   repetitive stuff was handled for you?"

stories.title: Checkr Made 900 Non-Coders Build Their Own AI Tools
stories.content:
Ninety-five percent daily adoption. That's what Checkr hit after one year of handing every employee a monthly stipend to try AI tools.

Checkr is a 900-person background check company. CEO Daniel Yanisse told Business Insider that the company went "all in" by giving every employee a budget to explore AI, then running company-wide AI days with hands-on demos. No mandates, no compliance training, just money and time to experiment. After a year of that, nearly everyone was prompting daily. So Yanisse pushed further and told staff in finance, legal, and HR to start vibe coding, which is basically describing what you want an app to do in plain English and letting AI build it for you.

They didn't just hand people Lovable and wish them luck. The company evaluated Cursor, Lovable, Replit, and Claude Code, then matched tools to skill levels. Lovable for total beginners. Cursor for people with some comfort around technology. And they stationed AI solution engineers on standby so when someone in accounting got stuck halfway through building a spreadsheet cleanup tool, they had someone to call.

That help desk piece is what most companies skip and it's the piece that makes everything else work. Yanisse put it simply: "They would come and help you and unstuck you if you have a problem, and take you all the way to success. And then you're on your way because then we share success stories with everyone in the company."

The same structure works whether you're running a 10-person team or a 200-person department. You don't need dedicated solution engineers. You just need one person who's a little further along to be the one others can ask. And the stipend thing is genuinely smart because it kills the most common excuse, which is that people don't have access to the good tools.

The Formula

1. Give everyone access. Pick one AI tool and make sure nobody has to pay out of pocket. Claude Pro is $20/month per person. That's the cost of one team lunch.

2. Run one AI day. Block a half day. Everyone brings a task they do over and over and tries getting Claude to help with it. No slides, just doing.

3. Pick a builder tool for beginners. Lovable is free to start and the easiest way for someone who's never coded to describe a simple tool they wish existed and actually build it.

4. Create a help channel. Slack channel, group chat, whatever you already use. When someone gets stuck they post there. When someone builds something useful they share it there.

5. Share wins company-wide. Checkr circulates success stories across the org. Nothing gets people to try something faster than seeing a coworker actually pull it off.

Have Claude Explain This to Me

Copy this prompt into Claude:

Checkr, a 900-person company, got 95% of employees using AI daily by
giving everyone monthly tool stipends, running hands-on AI days, and
then graduating non-technical staff to building their own apps with
beginner-friendly tools like Lovable. They matched tools to skill
levels and had internal help available when people got stuck.

Here's what Thorium Valley recommended:
- Give everyone access to at least one paid AI tool
- Run a hands-on AI day where people bring real repetitive tasks
- Introduce a beginner-friendly builder tool like Lovable for
  people who want to go beyond prompting
- Create a help channel and share wins publicly to build momentum

When I paste this, start by saying: "Hey! I have all the context
from Thorium Valley and heard you're trying to get your team
actually using AI instead of just talking about it. Could I get a
little more context on:
1. How big is your team, what kind of work do they mostly do, and
   how much AI experience do people have right now?
2. What's the main thing you're hoping AI adoption solves — is it
   speed, freeing people from repetitive work, reducing your
   engineering backlog, or something else entirely?"

stories.title: He Used Square's AI to Find a Hidden Best-Seller He Almost Cut
stories.content:
Donnie McClanahan was about to pull wraps and quesadillas off the menu at his cafés.

McClanahan runs five cafés in Knoxville, Tennessee, and he'd been operating mostly off instinct for years. With one location that's manageable. With five, you're guessing across hundreds of menu items, dozens of staff schedules, and thousands of transactions you'll never manually comb through. He figured tortilla-based items were underperforming compared to burgers and chicken, so trimming them felt obvious.

Then he asked Square AI to compare sales volume by lunch category. Wraps and quesadillas were selling almost identically to burgers. The real underperformer was the patty melt, which required a unique prep process and an ingredient (thousand island dressing) that nothing else on the menu used. He turned it into a seasonal special and kept the items that were quietly carrying the lunch rush.

"One of the most valuable things that Square AI has done for me is to help me avoid making a bad decision," McClanahan wrote.

The menu save was good. The labor savings were better. He asked Square AI for sales data broken down by hour and day of the week across all five locations, and one pattern jumped out immediately. One café was fully staffed for a window when basically nobody was walking in. He pushed that store's opening back 30 minutes and it had zero impact on service. After a year of tracking labor costs as a percentage of sales, he made similar scheduling tweaks across the board and reduced his labor cost percentage by ten full points.

The thing is, none of this data was new. It was already sitting in his POS system. He just never had a fast way to ask questions about it. And that's the part worth paying attention to, because whether you run a café or a consulting firm or a retail store, you probably have the same blind spots hiding in whatever system tracks your revenue.

The Formula

You don't need Square AI to do this. You need your sales data, a spreadsheet, and Claude.

1. Export your data. Pull your sales reports from whatever POS or invoicing system you use. Most systems (Square, Toast, Shopify, QuickBooks) let you export to CSV. Grab at least 90 days and make sure it includes timestamps, item names, and categories.

2. Drop it into Google Sheets. Upload the CSV so you have a clean, sortable version. Add a column for labor cost if your system doesn't include it, even rough estimates work.

3. Ask Claude to find what's hiding. Paste a sample of your data into Claude and ask it to identify your top revenue categories, flag items that look like underperformers but aren't, and spot time windows where sales don't justify staffing.

4. Make one change this week. Pick the single clearest insight and act on it. Adjust one opening time, cut one menu item that genuinely isn't pulling weight, or shift one staffing block. Small moves, real savings.

Have Claude Explain This to Me

Copy this prompt into Claude:

A multi-location café owner was making menu and staffing decisions based on
gut feeling. He exported his POS sales data, used AI to compare item
performance by category and analyze revenue by hour across locations, and
discovered a hidden best-seller he almost cut and a scheduling gap that
saved him 10 points on labor costs.

Here's the basic approach from Thorium Valley:
- Export 90+ days of sales data from your POS or invoicing system as a CSV
- Upload it to Google Sheets so it's clean and sortable
- Paste a sample into Claude and ask it to surface top revenue drivers,
  underperformers, and time windows where sales don't justify staffing
- Pick one clear insight and make a single operational change this week

title: 30 Tax Pros Built Working Software. None of Them Could Code.
intro:
Good Morning Thorium Valley, welcome back to the Catalyst Newsletter.

Today we're talking about 30 tax professionals who had zero coding experience, got handed AI tools for six weeks, and walked out with working software their firm actually uses with real clients.

We're also looking at a CPA who let an AI agent do his bookkeeping on camera, it processed 6,700 transactions in under eight minutes, and 150,000 accountants watched because they all wanted to know how.

And we're checking out a cowboy boot company that split its inventory in half, let AI manage one side and humans manage the other, and the AI side outsold the humans by nearly 10%.
toc: 30 Tax Pros Built Working Software. None of Them Could Code.
A CPA Let Claude Do His Bookkeeping. 150,000 Accountants Took Notes.
This Boot Company Let AI Manage Half Its Inventory. It Outsold the Human-Managed Half by 9.6%.

stories.title: 30 Tax Pros Built Working Software. None of Them Could Code.
stories.content:
KPMG handed 30 of its tax professionals access to AI coding tools and gave them six weeks. By the end, they had built automation tools that the firm now uses with actual clients.

The participants had two to six years of tax experience and limited technical backgrounds. They worked in small teams of four to six alongside engineers, using AI-powered "vibe coding" platforms that turn plain English descriptions into working software. A manager from KPMG's tax tech team coached each group through the snags.

What they built was practical stuff: tools that automated compliance processes, pulled data from multiple systems, and generated analytics that used to take hours of manual effort. Brad Brown, KPMG's chief digital officer for tax, said that before the pilot, a tax pro who wanted a specific tool built had to wait in line for engineering resources. Now they could take a first pass themselves and hand off a working prototype for engineers to polish and secure. "Right before your eyes, you're starting to see the evolution of how they were going to deliver services," he said.

KPMG is now considering forming about a dozen permanent teams of around 30 people each, mixing tax staff and engineers, to keep building this way.

The idea here isn't really about tax. It's that the people closest to a problem are now able to build the fix, and the tools to do it are available to basically anyone. If you spend hours every week on some repetitive process you could describe in plain English, you're closer to automating it than you think. That goes whether you're in accounting, operations, client services, or really anything where you keep doing the same sequence of steps and wishing something would just handle it for you.

The Formula

1. Pick one workflow that makes you groan. Not the most complex thing you do. The most repetitive. The thing where you think "there should be a tool for this" at least once a week.

2. Write out every step in plain language. Open a Google Doc and describe exactly what you do, start to finish. What data goes in, what comes out, where you copy-paste between systems. Be specific about it.

3. Bring it to Claude and ask what it can build you. Paste your workflow description and say "I want to automate as much of this as possible. What's the simplest tool you could build me?" Claude can generate working Google Sheets templates, Notion databases, or lightweight web apps you just open in your browser.

4. Test it on real work and tell Claude what's wrong. The first version won't be perfect. Use it once, note what's off, paste your feedback back in. Two or three rounds of this and you'll have something genuinely useful.

5. Share it with your team. If it works for you, it probably works for the person next to you doing the same thing every week.

stories.title: A CPA Let Claude Do His Bookkeeping. 150,000 Accountants Took Notes.
stories.content:
Jason Staats is a CPA with a YouTube channel called Jason On Firms where he helps accountants run better practices. A few weeks ago he posted a video walking through Claude CoWork, Anthropic's desktop AI agent, doing real bookkeeping on his computer. Over 150,000 accountants watched it in three weeks, which tells you something about how hungry the profession is for this.

The numbers were the headline. He fed CoWork 6,700 bank transactions and a simple Excel template, told it to enter and classify everything, and it finished in 7 minutes and 29 seconds. The ending balance matched the bank statement. The classifications looked like what a human bookkeeper would do. He started smaller first, 67 transactions then 670 then 6,700, scaling up as he built what CoWork calls "skills," which are basically reusable instructions that teach the agent patterns. He made one that builds a vendor map on the fly so Claude doesn't have to think about Home Depot every single time it shows up and just auto-classifies it going forward. That one skill cut processing time on a 670-transaction file from 12 minutes to about 3.

He also showed it matching 41 receipts to their transactions and renaming the files in about 60 seconds. For tax prep, he dropped 57 pages of tax documents into CoWork with an Excel 1040 workpaper and it made 349 entries like a seasoned preparer would. When he planted 10 deliberate errors and told it to check its own work, it caught nine.

The honest part, and what made the video credible, is that Staats was upfront about the limits. CoWork runs locally on your desktop but the AI models are still in the cloud, so sensitive data leaves your machine. His advice was blunt: don't use real client files until the security picture improves. He built AI-generated fake bank statements and receipts for every single demo. The Max plan runs about $200 a month and heavy daily use pushes costs higher, but as Staats put it, humans cost a lot more.

The reason this hit with 150,000 people isn't that bookkeeping is thrilling. It's that most knowledge work has a version of this same problem, a pile of data that needs to be sorted, categorized, matched, or entered somewhere. If you're reconciling invoices, organizing expense reports, processing survey responses, or doing any kind of repetitive data entry, the same approach works. Point an AI agent at the files, give it a template, let it handle the part that doesn't need your brain.

The Formula

1. Get Claude CoWork from claude.ai on a paid plan. Pro works for light use but anything serious will want Max.

2. Build a test dataset. Don't start with real company or client data. Export a sample spreadsheet or ask Claude to generate realistic test transactions for you.

3. Create your template. Make the spreadsheet or document you want the finished product to look like, with columns, categories, and any classification logic written out clearly.

4. Write your first prompt. Drop in both the source files and the template, then something like "Enter all transactions from these files into this template and classify them to the best of your ability." Start small and scale up.

5. Turn patterns into skills. Once Claude figures out a good workflow, tell it to save that as a skill. Next time you run the same type of task it already knows the playbook and works faster.

Have Claude Explain This to Me

Copy this prompt into Claude:

A CPA named Jason Staats demonstrated using Claude CoWork to automate

minutes by having CoWork enter and classify them into a spreadsheet
template, match receipts to transactions, and prepare tax workpapers
from source documents. He built reusable "skills" in CoWork to speed
up repeated tasks like vendor classification.

Here's the basic approach from Thorium Valley:
- Start with a test dataset, not real sensitive data
- Create a clear template showing what the finished output looks like
- Give CoWork your source files and template with simple instructions
- Build skills for any workflow you'll repeat so it gets faster each time
- Review everything before trusting it, accuracy was strong but not perfect

stories.title: This Boot Company Let AI Manage Half Its Inventory. It Outsold the Human-Managed Half by 9.6%.
stories.content:
Tecovas sells cowboy boots. Not software, not SaaS, not anything that sounds like it belongs in an AI case study.

The company has about 60 retail stores and a 10-year track record of doing things the old-fashioned way, which included managing inventory with spreadsheets and manual allocation. Someone on the team would look at what sold where and decide which boots to send to which store. It worked fine until it didn't scale.

So Tecovas tried something simple. They partnered with a company called Invent.AI and let the AI manage inventory decisions for some product categories while humans kept managing others. Same stores, same time period, direct comparison.

The AI-managed categories brought in 9.6% more revenue. They also had a 2% better in-stock rate and a 20% increase in new product sales. The AI was better at figuring out which specific boot in which specific size should go to which specific store to maximize the chance someone actually buys it.

"It's completely changed the way we manage our most important asset in retail, which is our inventory," Kevin Harwood, the company's CTO, said at Shoptalk Spring.

The interesting part isn't that AI beat humans at inventory allocation. It's that Tecovas set up the experiment to find out. They didn't just adopt AI and hope for the best. They ran it side by side with their existing process and measured the gap. That's something anyone can do whether you're managing product inventory, a content calendar, purchasing decisions, or even staffing schedules. Pick a category, let AI handle the recommendations, keep doing the other ones yourself, and compare notes after a month.

The Formula

1. Pick one recurring decision you make with a spreadsheet. This could be what to reorder, what content to publish, which leads to prioritize, what to schedule. Anything where you're looking at data and making a call repeatedly.

2. Build a simple tracking sheet. Open Google Sheets or Airtable and create two tabs: "AI Recommended" and "My Call." Log the same type of decision in both, along with whatever outcome matters to you like revenue, engagement, completion rate, or response time.

3. Feed your data into Claude and ask for recommendations. Take your historical data, paste it in, and ask Claude to recommend what you should do next based on the patterns. Do this for half your decisions. Make the other half yourself the way you normally would.

4. Run it for 30 days and compare. At the end of the month, look at both tabs. Which set of decisions performed better and by how much? You're not trying to prove AI is smarter. You're trying to see where it adds value for your specific work.

others, then compared results. The AI-managed categories outperformed by 9.6%
in revenue with better in-stock rates.

Here's the basic approach from Thorium Valley:
- Identify one recurring decision you currently make using spreadsheets or gut feel
- Create a simple tracking sheet that logs both AI-recommended and human decisions
- Feed your historical data into Claude and ask for pattern-based recommendations
- Run both approaches side by side for 30 days and compare outcomes

2. What does your current process look like for those decisions, and what

stories.title: This Marketing Team's Help Center Videos Used to Take Hours. Now It's 10 Minutes.
stories.content:
Owner.com's VP of Marketing, David Fallarme, did something kind of brilliant. He made his marketing team present AI projects to each other.

He called it an AI science fair, and the format was simple. Everyone picks a workflow that's annoying, builds something with AI to fix it, then shows the team what they made. Three projects came out of it, ranked by difficulty, and the easiest one might be the most useful.

Haley Smith, one of the marketers on the team, tackled help center videos. If you've ever made these, you know the drill. You write a script, record a Loom, re-record it because you fumbled a sentence, edit it, and an hour later you have one video that maybe 40 people will watch. Smith built a custom GPT that takes internal docs and standardizes them into a script, then ran that script through an AI voiceover tool layered on top of a screen recording. New time per video: 10 minutes.

The other two projects were more advanced. Fallarme himself built a workflow that takes sales call recordings, sends customized summaries to Slack through Zapier, converts them to audio with ElevenLabs, and drops the MP3 back in Slack so he can listen to "podcasts" about his sales process while walking his dog. And another teammate built a dashboard you can literally talk to, where you ask Claude questions like "what video got the most engagement on Facebook in October?" and get answers instantly because all the data lives in one place.

The help center video project is the one worth stealing though, because anyone can do it today and the pain it solves is universal.

The Formula

1. Pick your most repetitive video type. Help center explainers, onboarding walkthroughs, feature tutorials, whatever you keep re-recording.

2. Build a custom GPT in Claude (or ChatGPT) with your docs. Upload your internal documentation, style guide, and a couple example scripts.

3. Record your screen doing the walkthrough. No voiceover, no pressure. Just click through the process in silence.

4. Layer AI voiceover on top. Tools like ElevenLabs or Descript can take your script and generate a natural-sounding voiceover.

5. Batch them. Once the system works, knock out five in a sitting.

stories.title: He Built an AI Agent That Preps All His Client Meetings. It Saves Him 5 Hours a Week.
stories.content:
Dave McCann talks to about ten clients a week.

McCann is a global managing partner at IBM Consulting, responsible for thousands of client relationships including Nestlé, Ericsson, and Riyadh Air. Before every meeting, his team used to spend 30 minutes pulling together a briefing doc and hopping on a prep call. Multiply that by ten meetings and you're looking at five hours a week just getting ready to have conversations.

So he built an AI agent he named after himself. Digital Dave scans his calendar, spots the upcoming client meetings, pulls internal data on project status and services sold, checks external sources like annual reports and market news, and then generates a list of ten things McCann needs to know before walking in.

The part that makes this interesting for everyone else is that McCann's problem is incredibly common. If you manage accounts, run a team, or just have a calendar full of meetings where you're expected to show up informed, you're probably doing some version of this prep work manually.

McCann also freed up three or four staffers who used to spend hours assembling those briefings. They now do other work.

The Formula

1. Build a meeting brief template. Open a Google Doc and write out what you'd actually want to know before any meeting.

2. Create a Claude Project for meeting prep. Paste your brief template into the Project instructions.

3. Feed it what you've got before each meeting. Paste in your last email thread, notes from previous meetings, and recent context.

4. Ask Claude to generate the brief. Something like "Based on everything here, write me a meeting brief using the template."

5. Do this for a week and notice what changes.

Copy this prompt into Claude:

client meeting, times ten meetings a week. He built an AI agent that scans

freed up several staffers from prep work.

Here's the basic approach from Thorium Valley:

  last discussion, company news, open questions, and opportunities
- Set up a Claude Project with that template in the instructions
- Before each meeting paste in email threads, past notes, and any

- Ask Claude to generate a structured brief you can scan in two minutes

stories.title: She Cut Her Proposal Process From a Week to a Day Using Two Free AI Tools
stories.content:
Adebukola Ajao runs B.D.Y. CONSULT, a full-service marketing agency, completely by herself.

She's done it for a decade. Every client strategy, every creative direction call, every partnership and piece of marketing execution lands on her desk because there is no other desk. That setup works great until you need to write a new client proposal, which used to eat an entire week of her life.

About two years ago she started feeding her discovery call notes, emails, and Google Docs into AI and asking it to draft proposals using templates she'd already built. The whole process now takes a day or less, according to Business Insider.

The part that caught our attention was how she uses Read AI to analyze her prospect calls. It doesn't just transcribe what people said, it picks up on engagement and body language throughout the conversation. So if a prospect leaned in when she mentioned influencer strategy but checked out during the pricing section, she knows exactly which parts of her proposal to double down on.

"If a client says no, I don't feel burned out from having spent a week doing their proposal," Ajao told Business Insider. "It's just onto the next one."

The Formula

1. Record your next client or prospect call. Use Read AI, Otter, or even just Zoom's built-in transcription.

2. Write one reusable proposal template. Lay out the sections you use every time.

3. Paste the transcript and template into Claude. Ask it to fill in the template using what the prospect actually said.

4. Edit the 30% that needs you. Your job is voice, strategy, and the judgment calls.

5. Repeat and refine. Save your best proposals as examples for next time.

title: A Window Cleaner Is Using AI as His CFO for $40 a Month
intro:
Good Morning Thorium Valley, welcome back to the Catalyst Newsletter.

Today we're talking about a window cleaner who pays $40 a month for ChatGPT and Claude and uses them like a full finance team, and honestly his approach to prepping for his accountant is something every small business owner should steal.

We're also looking at how one company's engineering team spun up 80 AI agents inside Notion, none of them took more than five minutes to build, and now one guy walks into meetings knowing everything that happened overnight without reading a single Slack thread.

And we've got a CMO who got tired of her team "using AI" without actually changing how they work, so she mapped out 700 daily tasks across her whole marketing org and cut a 50-step campaign process down to 11.

stories.title: A Window Cleaner Is Using AI as His CFO for $40 a Month
stories.content:
Kyle Ray runs a window cleaning company and his entire C-suite is artificial intelligence.

Ray is the founder of Geek Window Cleaning, a side hustle he grew into a six-figure business. He pays $40 a month for ChatGPT and Claude and uses them the way a bigger company would use a finance team. He asks them to surface tax strategies, prep questions for his CPA, and double-check what his accountant sends back. One of his go-to prompts is basically just "what questions am I not asking that I should be asking?" which is honestly the most useful thing you could type into any AI tool.

The part that caught our attention is what happened when he started comparing his own AI-assisted tax prep against his accountant's work. He would bring the discrepancies back to his CPA and sometimes they would say yeah, good catch, you can do that. Other times they would explain why he couldn't. Either way he was having a better conversation than he would have had walking in cold.

His CPA Amanda Han actually validates the approach for the basics. AI is great at explaining what depreciation is or how an S corp works, she told Business Insider. But when it comes to something like "is an S corp right for me specifically," that still needs a human. The line is pretty clear and it applies to basically any professional service. AI can get you 80% prepared so the expert you're paying spends their time on the 20% that actually requires judgment.

The $40 a month thing is what makes this worth paying attention to. A part-time bookkeeper runs $250 a month minimum. A quarterly CPA consultation is $400 to $600 a pop. Ray isn't replacing his accountant, he's just showing up way more prepared, which means he gets more value out of every hour he pays for. And the same approach works whether you're running a cleaning company, a consulting practice, a restaurant, or really any small business where you're the one staring at the books.

The Formula

1. Gather your financial docs. Pull together last year's tax return, your recent bank statements, and any receipts or expense records you have. Even messy is fine.

2. Open Claude and give it context. Tell it your business type, how you're structured (sole prop, LLC, S corp), your rough annual revenue, and your main expense categories. This is how it stops giving you generic answers.

3. Ask it to find what you're missing. Upload your tax return or paste in your expense categories and ask "what deductions or tax strategies might I be overlooking?" Then ask "what questions should I bring to my accountant?"

4. Prep a one-page CPA cheat sheet. Take Claude's output and organize it into a short list of questions and flagged items. Bring this to your next accountant meeting instead of showing up empty-handed.

5. After your CPA meeting, close the loop. Go back to Claude with what your accountant said. Ask follow-up questions while the conversation is fresh. Save the whole thread so you're not starting from zero next quarter.

- Give Claude your business structure, revenue range, and expense categories
- Upload or describe your financial docs and ask what you might be missing
- Generate a list of questions to bring to your next accountant meeting
- After the meeting, use Claude to follow up on what your CPA recommended

stories.title: Clay's Team Built 80 AI Agents in a Week. Each One Took 5 Minutes.
stories.content:
Five minutes per agent, no code, no hand-holding.

Clay is, ironically, a go-to-market data platform. The company helps other teams automate manual data work but they were drowning in their own coordination overhead. Willie Yao, Clay's head of engineering, kept finding out about customer issues hours after they'd already escalated. Details lived in a Slack thread somewhere but he couldn't monitor every channel personally. Meanwhile Yash Tekriwal, who runs education and community, was spending hours each week digging through call transcripts looking for customer insights.

Both problems came down to the same thing. The information existed, it just sat there doing nothing.

Clay had already centralized everything in Notion, meeting notes, projects, docs, all connected to Slack and Google Drive. So when Notion rolled out Custom Agents, the team had a head start. All that context was already organized and waiting. Within a week they had 80+ agents running in the background across the entire company.

There were three that did a lot of the heavy lifting. First, the Meeting Classifier, which reads transcripts and figures out if something is a one-on-one, a team meeting, or all-hands, then files everything in the right place automatically. Second, the Incident Manager, which watches Slack for production issues and synthesizes what's happening, who's involved, and what to do next. "We realized that Custom Agents often do a better job when it comes to understanding what the root cause is," Willie said. And third, the Daily Briefer, which scans all of engineering's work every morning and pushes Willie a summary of active bugs, incidents, launches, and meetings to prep for. "People are surprised about the amount of context that I have," he said. "It's because I have this Custom Agent that's always looking out for me."

The setup was almost suspiciously easy. "I was shocked at how simple it was," Yash said. "I connected Slack, set up a prompt, and I was able to test the results in five minutes." And adoption spread entirely by word of mouth. Someone would ask Willie how he's tracking everything, he'd say Custom Agents, and that person would go build their own.

The real thing worth stealing here isn't the agents themselves but the pattern. If your team already keeps its work in one place, whether that's Notion or something similar, you're sitting on the same advantage Clay had. The meeting classifier idea works just as well for a project manager sorting client calls as it does for a community lead. The daily briefer is useful for anyone managing a team who's tired of manually piecing together what happened overnight.

The Formula

1. Pick one workflow that eats your time every week. Meeting notes piling up, status updates you compile by hand, messages you triage manually. Start with just one.

2. Make sure the information already lives in Notion. Agents need context to work with. If your meeting notes, project databases, or docs aren't in Notion yet, spend some time getting them there honestly.

3. Create a Custom Agent in Notion. Go to the Agents section in your sidebar, describe what you want in plain English, something like "read new meeting transcripts, classify them by type, and file them in the right database." Notion will generate the instructions and triggers for you.

4. Set a trigger and limit the access. Choose when the agent should run, like when a new page hits your meetings database or every morning at 9 AM. Only give it access to the specific pages and databases it actually needs.

5. Test it with real examples, then let it run. Trigger it manually a few times, check the output, adjust the instructions if something's off, and then turn it loose. Check back after a week to see if it's actually saving you time before building the next one.

Have Claude Explain This to Me

Copy this prompt into Claude:

A fast-growing startup had useful information scattered across Notion,
Slack, and Google Drive but no one could act on it fast enough. They
built 80+ Custom Agents inside Notion that automatically classify
meeting notes, monitor Slack for issues, and generate daily briefings,
each one set up in about 5 minutes with zero code.

Here's the basic approach from Thorium Valley:
- Identify one repetitive workflow you do manually every week
- Make sure the relevant info already lives in Notion
- Create a Custom Agent using plain English instructions
- Set a trigger (new database entry, schedule, Slack message) and
  limit the agent's access to only what it needs
- Test with real data before expanding

When I paste this, start by saying: "Hey! I have all the context from
Thorium Valley and heard you're trying to set up AI agents to automate
some of the repetitive work on your team. Could I get a little more
context on:
1. What does your team use for documentation and project management
   right now, and is most of your work already living in Notion?
2. What's the one recurring task that eats the most time each week,
   like compiling updates, sorting through notes, or triaging
   messages?"

stories.title: She Mapped Every Task Her Marketing Team Does. 80% Could Be Done by AI.
stories.content:
Teresa Barreira is the CMO of Publicis Sapient, the tech consulting arm of ad giant Publicis. Three years ago she told her marketing team to start using AI and experiment with it. Six months later she checked in to see how their work had changed. And you probably already guessed it, nothing changed. They were all "using" AI in the sense that they'd ask it to help write emails or brainstorm headlines, but the actual workflows, the sequence of who does what and when and how many people touch something before it ships, were identical.

So she took a first-principles approach. Her team mapped every single function across the entire marketing org and catalogued over 700 tasks they perform daily. The results were kind of brutal. Between 80% and 90% of those tasks could be accelerated or fully handled by AI. About 40% could run end-to-end with AI agents and no human in the loop at all.

The most concrete example is campaign launches. Her team puts out about five campaigns a month, and getting one to market used to require around 50 handoffs, people talking to people, approvals sitting in queues, files bouncing between tools. After redesigning the process around what AI could handle, they got it down to 11 steps.

The part that actually matters though is what she did next. She rewrote job descriptions for every function to focus on the 20% of work that only humans can do. Judgment, intuition, pattern recognition, the ability to go against the grain when the data says one thing but your gut says another. As Barreira put it, "AI is not going to be as brave as humans are."

This approach works whether you run a marketing team of 50 or you're one person trying to figure out where AI fits into your day. The exercise is the same. Write down what you actually do, be honest about how much of it is just coordination and production, and you'll probably find the ratio isn't that different from hers.

The Formula

1. Open a Google Sheet and list every task you do in a week. Column A is the task, Column B is who does it, Column C is how often, Column D is roughly how long it takes. Spend some time filling this in honestly. Don't write what your job description says, write what you actually do.

2. Score each task for AI-readiness. Add a Column E and mark each one as "AI can do this," "AI can help with this," or "only a human can do this." Be ruthless. If the task is mostly copying information between tools or following a checklist, it's probably in that first bucket.

3. Find your 50-to-11 moment. Pick the workflow with the most handoffs or steps and sketch out what it would look like if AI handled the parts you just flagged. You're looking for the steps where a person is basically acting as a middleman between two systems.

4. Rebuild one workflow first. Use Zapier to connect the tools involved and let it handle the routing and notifications automatically. Don't try to automate everything at once. Get one workflow running cleanly and learn from it.

5. Rewrite your own job description around the 20%. Once you see what AI can take off your plate, define what you should actually be spending time on. That's the whole point.

Have Claude Explain This to Me

Copy this prompt into Claude:

A CMO at a major consulting firm found that her team was using AI but
hadn't changed any of their actual workflows. She mapped all 700+ daily
tasks across her marketing org and discovered 80-90% could be accelerated
by AI, with 40% running fully autonomously. She then cut campaign launches
from 50 handoffs to 11 steps and rewrote every job description around the
20% of work only humans can do.

Here's the basic approach from Thorium Valley:
- List every task you do in a week in a spreadsheet with who does it,
  how often, and time spent
- Score each task as "AI can do this," "AI can help," or "human only"
- Find the workflow with the most handoffs and redesign it with AI
  handling the flagged steps
- Use Zapier to connect your tools and automate routing and notifications
- Redefine your role around the work that actually requires human judgment

When I paste this, start by saying: "Hey! I have all the context from
Thorium Valley and heard you're trying to figure out which parts of your
work AI can actually take over. Could I get a little more context on:
1. What's your role and what does a typical week look like for you in
   terms of the types of tasks you spend the most time on?
2. What's the workflow that frustrates you the most right now, the one
   with too many steps or too many people involved before something
   actually gets done?"
